MARKET OVERVIEW
🌎 Wall Street bought the bonds and dumped the stock.

Track every space stock live at Orbit Alpha

Two weeks ago the Fed gatecrashed the party. Last week the macro did the damage. This week the sector did something stranger: it staged its single strongest run of company-level catalysts since it began trading as a group, a $25 billion bond deal, a flawless launch, a NASA award, a sovereign satellite contract, and the prices fell anyway, in some cases hard. The disconnect between what the companies are doing and what their shares are doing has rarely been this wide.

SpaceX priced a $25 billion inaugural bond offering to institutional investors who oversubscribed it 3.5-to-one, then the equity printed a post-IPO low the same day. MDA banked a C$688 million sovereign satellite contract. Rocket Lab flew its 91st mission at 100% success and won a NASA award for three more. AST confirmed its next satellite batch for August. And every one of those names still finished the week lower, because the sell-off that began with the SpaceX IPO rotation and the Fed's hawkish turn has become self-reinforcing, margin calls, crowded exits and forced selling in a thin-float group feeding on themselves regardless of the tape underneath.

The names with funded paths and calendar-locked catalysts were repriced on sentiment, not fundamentals. The names whose 2026 run was built mostly on momentum, with no cushion, fell hardest of all. The broad market was actually risk-on for much of the week on US–Iran de-escalation, which means the space sell-off was, once again, the sector trading against the tape rather than with it.

SPACEX (SPCX)

The bond deal was a huge transaction for SpaceX, and it is bigger than the share price. The five-tranche $25 billion issue, $7bn at 5.35% (2031), $6bn at 5.65% (2033), $6bn at 5.875% (2036), $2.5bn at 6.60% (2046), $3.5bn at 6.65% (2056), retires the September 2027 bridge cliff entirely and terms out SpaceX's debt to maturities no nearer than five years away. SpaceX disclosed alongside it that it holds just over $100 billion in cash. The index committees weren't done either - Nasdaq confirmed SPCX will join the Nasdaq-100 on 7 July (an event expected to drive roughly $4.3 billion in passive inflows), and the stock was also added to the Russell 1000 at the June reconstitution. And yet the equity fell for most of the week, bottoming at $147.11 before stabilising near $153. The bear case has a number now too, Morningstar's fair value sits at $62, and Argus initiated at Hold on 26 June, arguing it will take years for the multiple to normalise. The tension is no longer abstract: credit and index inclusion are pulling one way, valuation the other, with the late-July lockup trigger and the 2 September earnings the next pressure points.

ROCKET LAB (RKLB)

Rocket Lab is the cleanest illustration of fundamentals and price diverging. Operationally it had an excellent week. On 24 June, NASA selected Rocket Lab for three dedicated Electron launches, two for the PolSIR ice-cloud mission and one for TSIS-2, under the $300 million VADR contract, with NASA explicitly citing Electron's 90-plus-flight heritage, deployment accuracy and seven-month turnaround as the deciding factors. On 27 June (NZST), Rocket Lab flew "Ten Owl of Ten," its 10th consecutive Synspective mission at 100% success, placing a StriX radar satellite into a 552 km orbit, its 12th launch of 2026 and 91st overall, with 18 further Synspective flights already booked. KeyBanc upgraded the stock to Overweight with a $135 target, and 15 of 19 covering analysts rate it Buy against a ~$107 consensus. The shares did the opposite of all that: having entered the Nasdaq-100 at Monday's open, RKLB sold the news, fell roughly 10% on the session, and kept sliding to close the week near $80, down about 25% on the week and over 40% on the month. A textbook case of a passive-inclusion "buy" event being swamped by a sector unwind.

AST SPACEMOBILE (ASTS)

AST gave the basket its one genuine reversal. On 22 June the company announced that BlueBirds 11, 12 and 13 are targeted for an orbital launch in the first half of August, the next batch in the cadence toward the ~45-satellite continuous-coverage threshold. The stock nonetheless kept bleeding with the group, touching an intraday low of $63.72 on Thursday (down more than 50% from its 28 May high of $133.86), before staging a sharp roughly 10% reversal on Friday 26 June on heavy call volume, closing the week around $71.45. Two competitive datapoints landed the same day and cut both ways: the FCC's wireless spectrum auction results named Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile and SpaceX among the winning bidders, and the FT reported SpaceX is weighing a Starlink-branded consumer mobile service in the US, a reminder that AST's direct-to-device runway is being contested by the same company now launching its satellites.

MDA SPACE (MDA)

While the high-multiple names unwound, MDA kept doing what differentiates it: converting government relationships into funded backlog. On 24 June the Canadian Space Agency concluded a contract with MDA, valued at approximately C$688 million, for a next-generation sovereign Earth-observation satellite that MDA will design, build, test, launch and commission as a replenishment to Canada's existing constellation. Coming directly on the heels of last week's debt-funded Blue Canyon acquisition, it reinforces the through-line on this name: where most of the basket is still spending to prove a model, MDA is being paid, by sovereign customers, on long-dated programs, to execute one it has already proven. In a week defined by a sentiment-driven sell-off, that distinction is the entire investment case.

VIRGIN GALACTIC (SPCE)

On 22 June, Virgin Galactic entered a privately negotiated exchange agreement with a holder of its 2.50% convertible senior notes, routine liability management aimed at trimming dilution and debt ahead of its Delta-class testing timeline, not an operational catalyst. The stock continued to trade on broader sector beta through the week.

Takeaway: This was the week the sector's two markets, credit and equity, openly disagreed. Institutional bond investors oversubscribed SpaceX's debt 3.5-to-one and the index committees added it to two benchmarks, all while the equity round-tripped from $225 to $147 and dragged the basket down 25–50% from recent highs. Strip out the price action and the fundamental ledger for the group is arguably stronger than it was a month ago. SpaceX retired its bridge-loan risk, Rocket Lab posted a flawless launch and a NASA win, MDA banked a sovereign contract, AST confirmed its next deployment. Whether that gap closes by prices recovering toward the fundamentals, or by the fundamentals proving the bears' valuation case right, is the question that the August lockup unlock and the next earnings cycle will start to answer. For now, the most reliable signal in the sector isn't the stock tape, it's the $89 billion that lined up to buy the bonds.

SENTIMENT SIGNAL
🎯 READING THE OTHER MARKET: WHAT SPACEX'S $25BN BOND TOLD EQUITY INVESTORS

This week handed the sector a genuine puzzle. SpaceX sold $25 billion of bonds into roughly $89 billion of orders, a 3.5x oversubscription, one of the largest investment-grade order books of the year, and its shares spent the same week pinned near a post-IPO low, a third below their June high. The lazy read is that smart credit money bought while jittery equity money sold. The accurate read is more useful, and more uncomfortable: both markets were pricing the same fact, and the bond deal handed equity holders the clearest disclosure yet of what they actually own. For a readership that is almost entirely equity-only, learning to read the credit side is an edge, so this week's deep dive is a guided tour of the other market.

OVERSUBSCRIPTION IS NOT ENDORSEMENT

Starting with the $89 billion headline, because it is the most misread number of the week. A 3.5x-covered book looks like a standing ovation. Look closer and it isn't one. SpaceX's benchmark 10-year note priced at 1.4 percentage points over Treasuries, and by Thursday, two days later, it had already widened to 1.57 points, meaning the bonds fell in the secondary market almost immediately. At the same time, dealers began making markets in SpaceX credit-default swaps, pricing five-year default protection at roughly 1.26% a year, nearly double the cost of protecting a similarly-rated peer like Intel at about 0.64%. The demand itself was mercenary: orders clustered at the short end where the spreads were fattest, with one investor summarising the mood as "a lot of extra spread for the ratings, but we are not taking a large order." It rented SpaceX for the yield, demanded a premium well above what the BBB-tier rating implied, and started buying insurance within 48 hours. The lesson generalises, a fat order book on a fat spread tells you the coupon was attractive, not that the credit is safe.

WHAT THE BOND ACTUALLY FIXED

Now the genuinely constructive part, because there is one. The proceeds retire SpaceX's $20 billion bridge loan in full, debt raised in March at an effective 4.58% to clean up the high-cost borrowings attached to the X and xAI deals, carrying a hard maturity in September 2027. That bridge was the single most concrete, near-term risk on the balance sheet, a deadline that had to be met regardless of where the stock traded. By refinancing it across maturities running from 2031 to 2056, SpaceX converted an acute refinancing cliff into a long-dated, scheduled obligation and secured permanent access to the investment-grade market (Moody's Baa1, Fitch BBB+, S&P BBB). This is the real signal for equity holders buried in a credit transaction: an existential "can they refinance in time?" question has been taken off the table. It is plausibly why the stock found a floor around $147 rather than continuing to slide, the nature of the risk changed from solvency to valuation.

WHAT THE BOND REVEALED

A bond sale of this size comes with disclosure, and the disclosure made SpaceX's capital intensity legible for the first time. S&P, the same agency that stamped it investment grade, simultaneously projects cumulative negative free cash flow approaching $230 billion between now and the end of 2029, even after assuming revenue quintuples, as space and AI spending overwhelm Starlink's profits. Goldman Sachs, the lead underwriter, separately models negative free cash flow of $105 billion in 2029 alone, with the business not turning cash-generative until around 2031. But the number that should matter most to anyone holding the equity is the one inside S&P's own model, to keep leverage in check against debt the agency sees climbing toward a quarter-trillion dollars by decade-end, it assumes SpaceX raises on the order of $150 billion of fresh equity over the period. The bond didn't just refinance a loan. It published the forward funding plan, and a large part of that plan is paid in dilution of the shares retail just bought.

WHY THE TWO MARKETS REACH DIFFERENT PRICES

This is the crux, and it is a concept worth carrying to every name in the basket. A bond is a senior, capped, time-bound claim. The holder gets paid before equity, receives a fixed coupon, and is repaid on a set date. To say yes, a credit investor needs one thing, confidence the company can service the debt. An equity share is a junior, uncapped, perpetual claim on whatever is left after everyone else is paid. To say yes at $153, an equity investor needs to believe in decades of compounding growth across launch, Starlink and AI. Those are different bars on the same company. Both markets actually agree on the foundation, Starlink, roughly 12 million subscribers and about $4 billion of operating profit in 2025, is the anchor, and every rating agency leaned on it as the linchpin of the investment-grade case. Where they part ways is everything above that floor: the AI and Starship spending that is consuming Starlink's profit today. Credit doesn't need that spending to pay off, it needs Starlink's cash to cover the coupon, a far lower bar that the agencies were willing to clear. Equity needs it to pay off emphatically, because the entire premium over Morningstar's $62 fair value estimate is precisely that optionality. Same company, same week, two defensible prices, because they are two different claims with two different bars.

THE SUPPLY WALL MAKES THE SPLIT CONCRETE

The cleanest illustration of the divergence is the share-supply picture, because the same fact carries opposite signs for the two markets. SpaceX floated only about 5% of its shares, roughly 95% unlock by December 2026, with an earlier partial trigger live into the Q2 print. So at the exact moment S&P is assuming SpaceX issues on the order of $150 billion of new equity, the existing locked supply is also coming to market. For a bondholder, more equity below you is more cushion, every dollar raised in stock is a dollar of loss-absorption ahead of the debt, which is good. For a shareholder, more equity is dilution and supply, which is bad. One event, two signs. If you ever want a single picture of why credit and equity are pricing SpaceX differently, that is it.

Takeaway: The bond deal was neither the ringing endorsement the $89 billion headline implied nor a reason for the equity's drop to read as panic. Both markets were doing the same thing, pricing, for the first time with hard numbers attached, a company that intends to consume cash on a national scale for the rest of the decade. Credit's verdict: we will lend, at a premium, and we will hedge, because Starlink covers the coupon and the 2027 cliff is gone. Equity's verdict: we will own the upside, but the bill is now visible, and part of it is paid in our own dilution. The single most valuable thing the bond gave equity investors wasn't $25 billion of refinancing, it was the disclosure of what they are really holding. The acute risk has been resolved; the chronic one just became impossible to ignore. The practical habit to take from it, watch the secondary bond spread and the CDS the way you watch the share price. When the credit market starts demanding a higher premium to hold the debt, as it quietly began to this week, it is often saying something about the equity that the stock tape has not yet caught up to.
